text: Second of May, two thousand and nine. The Santiago Bernabéu is full, and Real Madrid believe they are about to take the league back.
Ninety minutes later, their stadium is silent.
Real Madrid two. Barcelona six.
It's still one of the most famous results in the history of the Clásico. But the score isn't really the story.
The story is a single tactical idea — tried that night for the first time in a big game — that would go on to change how football is played.
To understand it, we need to go back a year, to a club that was falling apart.
Part one. A club falling apart.
In two thousand and six, Barcelona were champions of Europe, with Ronaldinho the most celebrated player on the planet.
Two years later, the dressing room had lost its hunger. The trophies stopped, the headlines were about nightlife, not football.
In the summer of two thousand and eight, coach Frank Rijkaard left, and the club decided to rebuild — moving on even some of its biggest stars.
Ronaldinho and Deco were sold. Even Samuel Eto'o was expected to leave — the new coach was reported to want a fresh start without him.
In the end, Eto'o stayed. It turned out to be one of the most important decisions of the season.
The question was who could lead the rebuild.

The club's choice surprised almost everyone. Pep Guardiola — a former Barça captain, just thirty-seven years old, whose only coaching experience was one season with the club's reserve team in the fourth tier of Spanish football.
He had won promotion with that B team. But in the first team, he had never managed a single game.
He arrived with a few simple rules. When you lose the ball, you win it back immediately — not in a minute, in a few seconds.
When you have the ball, every pass has a purpose: to move the opponent, to open a gap, not just to keep it.
And he trusted young players from the academy, including two he knew from the B team: Sergio Busquets and Pedro.
The start was a disaster. A defeat away to newly promoted Numancia, then a draw at home. People wondered if the club had made a terrible mistake.
Then the team barely stopped winning.
The attack was frightening. Messi, Eto'o and Thierry Henry would end the season with a hundred goals between them in all competitions.
But the real change was without the ball. Guardiola's Barça pressed like no big team in Spain had pressed before — six, seven players hunting the ball the second it was lost.
Part two. Madrid's comeback.
Real Madrid had their own crisis. In December, they sacked their coach and handed the job to Juande Ramos.
And under Ramos, Madrid went on one of the best runs of their recent history. Week after week they won, chasing Barça down the table.
By the start of May, after thirty-three games each, the gap was just four points.
And the next game was the Clásico, at the Bernabéu. Win it, and Madrid would be one point behind, with every bit of momentum on their side.
Madrid had another reason for confidence. Barça had a Champions League semi-final against Chelsea just four days after the Clásico — and some in Madrid believed Guardiola might rest players.
He didn't. He picked his strongest team, and he gave them a plan.
The Spanish press called it the match of the season. For Madrid, it was a chance to change everything.
Part three. The idea.
Here's what Guardiola and his staff had noticed about Madrid.
Their midfielders liked to push up and press. But their centre-backs stayed deep, protecting the space in front of their goalkeeper.
Between those two lines, there was a gap. And a normal centre-forward, standing between the defenders, would never use it.
So Guardiola moved Lionel Messi.
Messi started on the right wing, as usual. But during the game he moved into the middle, and dropped into that gap — while Samuel Eto'o went out wide.
Now Madrid's centre-backs had a problem. Follow Messi into midfield, and leave a hole behind them. Stay put, and let the best player in the world turn and run at them, unmarked.
Either way, the space behind them opened up for Thierry Henry and Eto'o.
A striker who doesn't stay where strikers stay. Football had seen the idea before — but never with a player like this, in a game this big.
Think about it from the Madrid bench. Every time a centre-back stepped up to Messi, Henry or Eto'o ran into the space behind him.
Every time he didn't, Messi turned and ran at the defence with the ball at his feet.
There was no good answer. And by the time Madrid realised that, the game was gone.
Part four. The match.
And it started badly. Fourteen minutes in, Sergio Ramos crossed from the right, and Gonzalo Higuaín headed Madrid in front.
The Bernabéu roared. For a few minutes, everything was going to plan.
Four minutes later, the idea paid off for the first time. Messi received the ball between the lines, and chipped it over the defence into Henry's run.
Henry was clean through. One–one.
Two minutes after that, Xavi swung in a free-kick, and the captain, Carles Puyol, headed it in.
Madrid had been ahead for six minutes. Now they were behind.
Then came the goal that summed up the night. Xavi stole the ball from Lassana Diarra near the halfway line, and slipped it to Messi.
Messi ran clear, with nobody close enough to stop him, and clipped the ball past Iker Casillas. Three–one at half-time.
Look at how the goal happened: Madrid's midfielders were pushing forward, their defenders were deep, and Messi was standing exactly in the space between them — the gap Guardiola had planned for.
In the dressing room, Madrid needed a response. Eleven minutes into the second half, they got one: Sergio Ramos headed in an Arjen Robben free-kick. Three–two.
For about two minutes, the comeback was on.
But Barça didn't panic. They did what Guardiola had trained them to do: keep the ball, move the opponent, wait for the gap to open again.
Then Henry scored again. Four–two.
With fifteen minutes left, Messi added his second. Five–two.
And in the closing minutes, Gerard Piqué — a centre-back, a boy from the club's own academy — walked forward and scored the sixth.
Real Madrid two. Barcelona six. At the Bernabéu.
The next morning, the league was effectively over. Barça were seven points clear with four games to play.
Part five. What it started.
What happened next is one of the greatest months in the club's history.
Four days after the Bernabéu, Andrés Iniesta scored in the ninety-third minute at Stamford Bridge to send Barça to the Champions League final.
A week later they won the Copa del Rey, and then the league title.
And on the twenty-seventh of May, in Rome, they beat Manchester United in the Champions League final. Messi — the false nine — scored with a header.
Samuel Eto'o — the striker the club had almost sold — scored the first after ten minutes.
Barça won the treble. By the end of the year, they had won six trophies out of six.
Six trophies in a single year. No Spanish team had ever done it before.
The sixth came in December, at the Club World Cup, when Messi scored the winner in extra time against Estudiantes.
Part six. The idea that spread.
What the two–six showed the world was that a centre-forward doesn't have to stay where centre-forwards stay.
By dropping into midfield, Messi created an extra man in the middle of the pitch — and forced defenders into a choice with no good answer.
Over the next decade, coaches across Europe built their teams around the same principle: forwards who drop, midfielders who run beyond them, and space created by movement rather than position.
A year later, Spain won the World Cup with a midfield built around Barça's players: Xavi, Iniesta and Busquets, with Puyol and Piqué behind them.
And Guardiola himself took the ideas to Bayern Munich and Manchester City, where they spread even further.
The false nine became one of the defining ideas of modern football. And for many people, it started on one night in Madrid.

It's easy to remember the two–six as a thrashing. But the people who were there remember something else: a team that had worked out a better way to play — and wasn't afraid to try it in the biggest game of the season.
So — is the two–six the greatest Clásico ever played? Or is there another night you'd put above it? Tell me in the comments.
And for what happened four days later, at Stamford Bridge — in the ninety-third minute — watch this next.
